lessons.title: Packages and crates
lessons.objective_md: Distinguish a package from its library and binary crates; identify their conventional roots and separate compilation boundaries.

screens.heading: A package describes the build

coming_from.c: A crate is the whole unit the compiler builds, like a library or executable target, not one `.c` file. There are no headers: the compiler finds the crate's other files by following declarations from the root.
coming_from.go: A Cargo package is close to a Go module with its `go.mod`. A crate is like a Go package that compiles to one library or one program, and `src/main.rs` plays the role of `package main`.
coming_from.java: A crate is roughly one compiled JAR or assembly, and the package is the project file that builds it. There is no per-class compilation: the compiler builds a whole crate starting from its root file.
coming_from.js: `Cargo.toml` plays the role of `package.json`: name, version and dependencies. Unlike an npm package, one Cargo package can produce a library crate and several executable crates, each compiled separately.
coming_from.python: A Cargo package is like a Python project with a `pyproject.toml`: the thing you build and share. A crate is closer to one importable package inside it, and Rust compiles each crate as a whole rather than file by file.

steps.caption_md: `Cargo.toml` describes a **package**: a bundle of one or more crates that Cargo builds together. The manifest names the package and its edition, but it contains no Rust code itself.
steps.visual_md: Package box "module-lab" (from Cargo.toml: name, version, edition); no crates inside it yet.

steps.caption_md: Cargo finds `src/main.rs` by convention and makes it the **crate root** of a binary crate with the package's name. A **crate** is the unit the compiler builds in one go, starting from its root file.
steps.visual_md: Package "module-lab" now contains one crate box: binary crate "module-lab", root src/main.rs.

steps.caption_md: A binary crate compiles to a program, so it must have a `main` function where execution starts. `cargo run` builds the crate and then calls this `main`.
steps.visual_md: Binary crate "module-lab" runs main; stdout: binary crate.

screens.heading: A library has a different crate root
screens.text_md:
`src/lib.rs` is the crate root of a **library crate**. A library has no `main`: it isn't run, it provides functions and types for other crates to call. The `pub` in front of `fn` lets those other crates see `double`; the next lesson explains it.

A package can contain at most one library crate. `cargo build` compiles it, but `cargo run` has nothing to run, because this package has no binary yet.

screens.heading: One package can contain both

steps.caption_md: With both root files present, Cargo builds **two crates** from one package: a library and a binary. Each has its own root file and its own module tree, even though they share the package's name.
steps.visual_md: Package "module-lab" contains two crate boxes: library crate module_lab (root src/lib.rs, item double) and binary crate module-lab (root src/main.rs, item main).

steps.caption_md: The binary reaches the library by the library's crate name, `module_lab`, just as it would reach any other crate. Cargo builds the library first and links it in, so the binary doesn't compile its own copy of `double`.
steps.visual_md: Arrow from binary crate main to library crate item double, labelled "module_lab::double".

steps.caption_md: `double(3)` runs the library's code and returns 6. Keeping the logic in the library and a thin `main` in the binary is a common layout, because other crates can reuse the library too.

question.prompt_md: A package contains only `Cargo.toml`, `src/lib.rs` and `src/main.rs`. How many crates does Cargo build from it?

options.text_md: One crate with two root files.
Two crates: a library and a binary.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. A crate has exactly one root file. Two root files means two crates; what they share is the package.
Correct. `src/lib.rs` is the root of the library crate and `src/main.rs` the root of the binary crate, both in one package.
Not quite. `src/main.rs` is a binary crate's root: it has `main` and compiles to a program. A package can have at most one library.

screens.heading: Several binaries, one library
screens.text_md:
Each file in `src/bin/` becomes another binary crate, named after the file. This package now has two binaries, `module-lab` and `admin`, and both use the one library.

With two binaries, a plain `cargo run` can't tell which program you mean, so it stops with an error. Name the binary instead: `cargo run --bin module-lab` prints `7`, and `cargo run --bin admin` prints `admin 7`.

screens.heading: Package names and Rust identifiers
screens.text_md:
Package names in `Cargo.toml` may contain hyphens, but Rust names can't: `module-lab::greeting()` would read as `module` minus `lab::greeting()`. So the library crate's name in Rust code replaces each hyphen with an underscore, `module_lab`.

The package name is for Cargo (the build, the binary's file name); the crate name is what Rust paths start with.

question.general_md: Correct. Only the binary's `main` runs on its own. The library's code runs when `main` calls `module_lab::setup()`, between the two other lines.

wrong_answers.why_md: Cargo compiles the library first, but compiling isn't running. Nothing in a library executes until a function in it is called.
the library's `println!` is ordinary code. When `main` calls `setup`, it prints just like code in `src/main.rs` would.

screens.heading: Choose the command for the task
screens.text_md:
`cargo build` compiles every crate in the package. `cargo check` checks them for errors without producing programs, which is faster while you edit. `cargo run --bin NAME` builds, then runs one binary.

`cargo test` builds the crates and runs their tests; here, that's how your practice solutions are checked. Writing your own tests is Chapter 11. None of these commands download anything when a package has no dependencies.

question.prompt_md: You add `src/bin/report.rs` to the package. What must the new file contain?

options.text_md: A copy of every library function it calls.
A second `Cargo.toml` describing the new binary.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `src/bin/report.rs` is the root of a new binary crate, and every binary crate starts running at its own `main`.
Not quite. The new binary calls the library through its crate name, `module_lab::...`, like the other binary does. Nothing is copied.
Not quite. Cargo finds files in `src/bin/` automatically; one `Cargo.toml` describes the whole package and all its crates.

summary: A package is what `Cargo.toml` describes; a crate is one unit the compiler builds from a single root file.
`src/main.rs` is the root of a binary crate, which needs `main`; `src/lib.rs` is the root of the package's one library crate.
Each file in `src/bin/` is another binary; with two or more binaries, choose one with `cargo run --bin NAME`.
A binary uses its package's library by crate name, with hyphens turned into underscores: `module_lab::double(3)`.

lessons.title: Modules and privacy
lessons.book_section: 7.2 Control Scope and Privacy with Modules
lessons.objective_md: Build a module tree and expose a public operation while keeping helper items private; explain descendant access.

screens.heading: Group related functions

steps.caption_md: `mod account { ... }` declares a **module**: a named container for related items. It becomes a child of the crate root, so the crate's items now form a tree.
steps.visual_md: Tree: crate (src/main.rs) → account. main shown as an item of crate.

steps.caption_md: `balance` lives inside `account`, so its name is `account::balance`. That keeps it from clashing with any other `balance` in the crate. `pub` lets code outside `account` call it.
`main` is in the crate root, where `account` is a child, so it can write the path `account::balance()`. Modules only organize names at compile time; nothing is created when the call runs.
steps.visual_md: Path highlight crate → account → balance; balance() returns 3; stdout: 3.

screens.heading: Modules can have children
screens.text_md:
Modules can contain other modules. `front_of_house` has two children, so the tree is `crate` → `front_of_house` → `hosting` and `serving`. The crate root is an implicit module named `crate` at the top.

A path follows the tree one `::` at a time. `hosting` and `serving` need `pub` too, because `main` has to pass through them.

screens.heading: Private is the default
screens.text_md:
Items in a module are **private** by default: only code inside that module, and inside its child modules, can use them. `main` is in the crate root, outside `pricing`, so the path stops at `helper`.

Privacy is checked at compile time, before the program ever runs. Writing `pub fn helper` would make the call compile.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0603]: function `helper` is private
 --> src/main.rs:8:29
  |
8 |     println!("{}", pricing::helper());
  |                             ^^^^^^ private function
  |
note: the function `helper` is defined here
 --> src/main.rs:2:5
  |
2 |     fn helper() -> u32 {
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

annotations.note_md: line 8: `main` is outside `pricing`, so it can't use `pricing`'s private items.
line 2: no `pub`, so `helper` is visible only inside `pricing` and its child modules.

question.prompt_md: Inside module `pricing`, which pair of declarations lets `main` call `pricing::quote()` while keeping `helper` hidden from `main`?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. This is reversed: `pub` goes on the item outside code may use. Here `main` could call `helper` but not `quote`.
Correct. Each item's visibility is chosen on its own. `quote` is `pub`, and it can still call its private sibling `helper` from inside `pricing`.
Not quite. `mod` declares modules, not functions. Neither line defines a function that `main` could call.

screens.heading: Expose an operation, keep a helper
screens.text_md:
`quote` is `pub`, so `main` can call it, and `quote` can call `helper` because both live in `pricing`. Outside code gets the operation it needs; the helper stays an implementation detail that `pricing` can change or remove without breaking any caller.

This is the usual pattern: make public only what callers should rely on.

coming_from.c: Like a `static` function in a `.c` file that only that file can call, while `quote` is the exported one. Rust applies this to modules at any nesting depth, and the compiler, not the linker, rejects outside calls.
coming_from.go: Go exports names that start with a capital letter. Rust uses the `pub` keyword instead, so `quote` stays lowercase. As in Go, the boundary is the module (Go's package), not a type.
coming_from.java: Rust has no class-level `private`: privacy is per module. Everything inside `pricing`, including its child modules, can call `helper`. Leaving out `pub` is closer to package-private, scoped to one module.
coming_from.js: Like an ES module, where only `export`ed names are visible outside the file, a Rust module shows only its `pub` items. But Rust modules can nest inside one file, and every path is checked at compile time.
coming_from.python: A leading underscore (`_helper`) is only a convention in Python; any caller can still use it. Rust enforces privacy: calling `pricing::helper()` from `main` doesn't compile. And everything is private until you write `pub`.

screens.heading: Children can use ancestor-private items
screens.text_md:
Privacy hides a module's items from code **outside** it, not from code nested inside it. `report` is a child of the crate root, so it can call the root's private `factor`. `super::` means "the parent module"; the next lesson covers it.

Child modules can see the context they are defined in. Parents can't see into their children's private items.

question.general_md: Correct. `pair` calls its private sibling `base` and doubles it: 10. `discount` is a child of `pricing`, so `super::base()` is allowed too: 5 - 1 = 4.

wrong_answers.why_md: `base` is private to `pricing`, but both callers are inside `pricing`: `pair` is a sibling and `discount` a child. Only code outside `pricing` is blocked.
`pair` returns `base() * 2`, not `base()` itself.

screens.heading: A public item can have a private ancestor
screens.text_md:
`run` is `pub`, but it sits inside `engine`, which is private to the library's root. The binary is a **different crate**, so it's an outsider: every module on the path must be visible to it, and `engine` isn't.

The library already offers a deliberate way in: `module_lab::start()` is public and calls `engine::run()` from inside the library.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0603]: module `engine` is private
 --> src/main.rs:2:32
  |
2 |     println!("{}", module_lab::engine::run());
  |                                ^^^^^^  --- function `run` is not publicly re-exported
  |                                |
  |                                private module
  |
note: the module `engine` is defined here
 --> src/lib.rs:1:1
  |
1 | mod engine {
  | ^^^^^^^^^^

annotations.note_md: `src/main.rs` line 2: the path passes through `engine`, which only the library's root can see.
`run` itself is `pub`, but a `pub` item is only reachable if every module on its path is too.

question.prompt_md: A library's root has `mod internals { pub fn run() {} }`. Another crate that depends on it calls `library::internals::run()`. Why doesn't it compile?

options.text_md: The path passes through `internals`, which is private to the library's root.
Only the library's own package binaries may call its functions.
The other crate must first write `use library::internals::run;`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `run` is `pub`, but every module on the path must be visible too, and `internals` has no `pub` (E0603).
Not quite. A binary in the same package gets no special access: it's a separate crate, like any other. Any crate can use public items through public paths.
Not quite. `use` only creates a shorter name for a path, and the same privacy check applies: the import would fail at `internals` too.

summary: `mod name { ... }` declares a module: a named container that becomes a child in the crate's module tree under `crate`.
Items are private by default; code outside a module can use only its `pub` items (E0603 otherwise).
Code inside a module, including its child modules, can use that module's private items.
Every module on a path must be visible to the caller; a `pub fn` inside a private module is still unreachable from another crate.

lessons.title: Paths
lessons.book_section: 7.3 Paths for Referring to an Item in the Module Tree
lessons.objective_md: Resolve crate, self and super paths; distinguish visibility of a type, its fields and enum variants.

screens.heading: Start an absolute path at the crate root

coming_from.c: `::` works like C++ namespace qualification, and `crate::` resembles a leading `::` for the global namespace. Unlike namespaces, each Rust module also hides its non-`pub` items from outside code.
coming_from.go: Go always names another package's items as `pkg.Func` after an import. Rust can write the full path inline, `crate::units::convert::twice`, and a path may pass through several nested modules.
coming_from.java: Like a fully qualified name such as `com.shop.units.Convert.twice`, written with `::`. Unlike Java packages, each module on the path has its own visibility, and the compiler checks every segment.
coming_from.js: There is no `../units` file path here. Rust paths walk the module tree, not folders, and `crate` names the root of that tree. You can call through a path inline, without an `import` line.
coming_from.python: `crate::units::convert::twice` is like the absolute import `from mypkg.units.convert import twice`, except you can call it inline without importing. `crate` always means the root of the crate being compiled, never a package name.

steps.caption_md: An **absolute path** starts with `crate`, the root of the crate being compiled; here, `src/main.rs`. The lookup starts at the top of the tree no matter where the calling code sits.
steps.visual_md: Tree: crate (src/main.rs) highlighted as the starting point; children units and main.

steps.caption_md: `units` isn't `pub`, but `main` can still name it. A private item is visible to code in the same module, and `main` and `units` are both items of the crate root.
steps.visual_md: crate → units highlighted; units has no pub tag; main is a sibling of units.

steps.caption_md: `convert` must be `pub`, because `main` is outside `units` and is looking inside it. Each segment of a path is checked on its own, so a path is only as visible as its least visible step.
steps.visual_md: crate → units → convert highlighted; convert has a pub tag.

steps.caption_md: `twice` is `pub` for the same reason. Every segment resolved and passed the privacy check, so the call compiles and prints 6.
steps.visual_md: crate → units → convert → twice highlighted; twice(3) returns 6; stdout: 6.

screens.heading: A relative path starts in the current module
screens.text_md:
A **relative path** starts from the module the code is written in. `main` is in the crate root, so `units::twice` finds `units` among the root's children: the same function as `crate::units::twice`.

The difference shows when the calling code moves. Move `main`'s code into another module and its relative paths start from there, so they may need updating; an absolute path to an item that stays put keeps working. The Book generally prefers absolute paths for that reason.

screens.heading: self and super describe a module position
screens.text_md:
`super::` starts a path in the parent module, like `..` in a file system: from inside `oven`, `super::base` is `kitchen::base`. `oven` is a child of `kitchen`, so it may use the private `base`.

`self::` starts in the current module, so `self::value` is the same as `value`; it's mostly useful in `use` lines. Both are module positions, unrelated to a method's `self` parameter.

question.prompt_md: Code inside module `parent::child` wants to call `helper`, a function defined directly in `parent`. Which path works?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `crate::child` looks for `child` at the crate root, but `child` is inside `parent`. The absolute path would be `crate::parent::helper()`.
Correct. `super` moves from `child` up to its parent, `parent`, where `helper` is defined. As a child, `child` may use `helper` even if it's private.
Not quite. `self` is the current module, `child`, so `self::child` would look for a module nested inside `child`.

screens.heading: A public struct can have private fields
screens.text_md:
`pub struct` makes the type public, but each field keeps its own visibility. `toast` is marked `pub`; `seasonal_fruit` isn't, so `main` may read `meal.toast` but not `meal.seasonal_fruit`.

This lets a module decide which parts of a value callers may touch: the kitchen chooses the fruit.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0616]: field `seasonal_fruit` of struct `Breakfast` is private
  --> src/main.rs:19:51
   |
19 |     println!("{} toast with {}", meal.toast, meal.seasonal_fruit);
   |                                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ private field

annotations.note_md: line 4: no `pub`, so only code inside `back_of_house` can read or set this field.

screens.heading: A private field blocks construction
screens.text_md:
`main` can get a `Breakfast` from `summer`, but it can't write a `Breakfast { ... }` literal: the literal would have to set `seasonal_fruit`, which is private to `back_of_house`.

So a struct with any private field needs a public **constructor**, an associated function such as `summer` defined inside the module, where the private field is visible.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0451]: field `seasonal_fruit` of struct `Breakfast` is private
  --> src/main.rs:26:9
   |
24 |     let custom = back_of_house::Breakfast {
   |                  ------------------------ in this type
25 |         toast: String::from("Wheat"),
26 |         seasonal_fruit: String::from("blueberries"),
   |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ private field

annotations.note_md: line 26: a struct literal must set every field, and `main` may not set `seasonal_fruit`.
line 24: the literal is written outside `back_of_house`, while `summer` on line 22 builds the value inside it.

screens.heading: The constructor is the way in
screens.text_md:
`summer` runs inside `back_of_house`, where `seasonal_fruit` is visible, so it can build the whole value and hand it back. Outside, `toast` is `pub`, so `main` can change it.

`seasonal_fruit` stays private. The public method `fruit` lets callers read it without being able to change it.

screens.heading: Public enum variants are all public
screens.text_md:
Enums work the other way round from structs: once an enum is `pub`, all its variants and their data are public. `main` can create `Soup` and `Salad(2)`, and `bowls` can match on them and read the `u32` inside.

An enum whose variants outside code couldn't name or match would be of little use, so Rust doesn't ask for `pub` on each variant.

question.general_md: Correct. `crate::OFFSET` starts at the crate root and finds 7. `super::OFFSET` starts at `inner`'s parent, `outer`, and finds 100. Both are private, but `inner` is nested inside both modules, so it may use them.

wrong_answers.why_md: `super` from `inner` is `outer`, not the crate root, so `super::OFFSET` is `outer`'s 100.
`crate::` always starts at the crate root. It doesn't pick the nearest module that defines `OFFSET`, so `crate::OFFSET` is 7.

screens.heading: The binary and library have different roots
screens.text_md:
Inside `src/main.rs`, `crate::` means the **binary** crate's root, so `crate::bonus` finds the `bonus` defined in this file. The library's items aren't under `crate::` here; the binary reaches them by the library's name, `module_lab::value`.

Inside `src/lib.rs`, `crate::value` would name the library's own function. Sharing a package doesn't merge the two module trees.

question.prompt_md: Module `stock` defines `pub struct Count { n: u32 }` and a public method `pub fn value(&self) -> u32`. Code outside `stock` has a `Count` called `count`. Which read compiles?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `n` has no `pub`, so it's private to `stock` even though the struct is public (E0616).
Correct. `value` is a public method defined inside `stock`, where `n` is visible, so it can return the private field.
Not quite. A struct's visibility and its fields' visibility are separate. Only enums make all their variants public.

summary: `crate::` starts a path at the root of the crate being compiled: the binary's root in `src/main.rs`, the library's in `src/lib.rs`.
A relative path starts in the current module; `super::` starts in its parent and `self::` in the module itself.
Every segment of a path must be visible from where the path is written.
A `pub struct` keeps its fields private unless each is `pub`; outside code then needs a public constructor (E0451) and can't read private fields (E0616).
A `pub enum` makes all of its variants public.

lessons.title: Bringing paths into scope with `use`
lessons.book_section: 7.4 Bringing Paths into Scope with the use Keyword
lessons.objective_md: Use local imports, aliases, nested use trees, globs and public re-exports without changing type identity or bypassing privacy.

screens.heading: Bring a module into scope

coming_from.c: Closer to a C++ `using` declaration or namespace alias than to `#include`: no text is pasted in. The compiler already sees the whole crate; `use` only adds a name to one scope.
coming_from.go: Like a Go import followed by `hosting.AddToWaitlist()`: the idiom keeps the package name at the call site. But Rust's `use` can name any module in the crate tree, not just whole packages.
coming_from.java: Like Java's `import` or C#'s `using`: a compile-time shortcut that doesn't change what a name refers to. Rust also lets you import a module and call through it, as in `hosting::add_to_waitlist()`.
coming_from.js: Similar to `import { hosting } from "./front_of_house"`, but `use` never loads a file. The module is already part of the crate through `mod`; `use` only adds a shorter name in this scope.
coming_from.python: Like `from front_of_house import hosting`, but nothing runs at import time: `use` only creates a name while compiling. The module itself exists because of its `mod` declaration, not because of the import.

steps.caption_md: `use` creates a shortcut: in this scope, the name `hosting` now means the module `crate::front_of_house::hosting`. It's like a symbolic link in a file system: nothing is copied and no code runs.
steps.visual_md: Tree: crate → front_of_house → hosting → add_to_waitlist. A dashed shortcut arrow from a new name "hosting" in the crate root's scope to the module crate::front_of_house::hosting.

steps.caption_md: The call still names the parent module, `hosting::`. That's the idiomatic style for functions: the path stays short, and a reader can see that `add_to_waitlist` isn't defined in this file's root.
steps.visual_md: The call hosting::add_to_waitlist() follows the shortcut arrow into the module, then to add_to_waitlist.

steps.caption_md: The shortcut was checked for privacy like a full path: `hosting` and `add_to_waitlist` are both `pub`. `use` only gives a shorter name; it never grants access.

screens.heading: Bring a type into scope
screens.text_md:
For structs and enums the idiom is the opposite: import the type itself and write `Point`, not `geometry::Point`. There's no strong reason, just convention, and it's what most Rust code does.

You've seen both styles: in Chapter 2, `use std::io;` imported a module (then `io::stdin()`), and `use std::cmp::Ordering;` imported a type. `use` never changes visibility: `x` and `y` are readable here only because they're `pub`.

screens.heading: Paths into other crates
screens.text_md:
A path can start with another crate's name. `std` is the standard library: a crate every Rust program can use without listing it anywhere. `std::cmp::Ordering` is the enum `Ordering` in module `cmp` of that crate.

Other external crates come from `[dependencies]` in `Cargo.toml`. In Chapter 2, adding `rand` there is what made paths starting with `rand::` work, such as `rand::rng()`.

screens.heading: An import belongs to one scope
screens.text_md:
A `use` adds its name to one scope: the module where it's written. Here that's the crate root, so `main` may call `twice(1)`. The child module `app` has its own, separate set of names, and `twice` isn't one of them.

The root's `use` acts like a private item of the root, which a child may see, so the compiler suggests `use crate::twice;`. Inside `app`, `use super::twice;` or the full path `crate::tools::twice(3)` work too.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0425]: cannot find function `twice` in this scope
  --> src/main.rs:11:9
   |
11 |         twice(3)
   |         ^^^^^ not found in this scope
   |
help: consider importing this function through its public re-export
   |
10 +     use crate::twice;
   |

annotations.note_md: line 11: inside `app`, the name `twice` was never introduced.
the suggested fix imports the root's shortcut into `app`; `use super::twice;` does the same.

question.prompt_md: A crate root contains `mod tools;` and `use crate::tools::run;`. What does a later call `run()` in the root do?

options.text_md: Calls the function `tools::run` that the crate already has.
Loads the file for `tools` a second time and calls its copy of `run`.
Calls `run` even if `run` is private, because `use` was written explicitly.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `use` makes `run` a second name for the existing function `crate::tools::run`. Nothing is copied.
Not quite. `mod tools;` is what brings the module into the crate, once. `use` doesn't load anything; it only adds a name.
Not quite. An import goes through the same privacy checks as a full path. If `run` were private, the `use` line itself would fail with E0603.

screens.heading: Two imports can't share a name
screens.text_md:
Each name in a scope can mean only one thing. Two different functions both imported as `value` would make `value()` ambiguous, so the compiler rejects the second import.

The idiomatic fix for functions is to import their parent modules instead and call `a::value()` and `b::value()`. Or rename one import, as the help suggests; the next screen shows how. The extra warning only says the rejected import was never used.

   |
13 | use crate::a::value;
   |     --------------- previous import of the value `value` here
14 | use crate::b::value;
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `value` reimported here
   |
   = note: `value` must be defined only once in the value namespace of this module
help: you can use `as` to change the binding name of the import
   |
14 | use crate::b::value as other_value;
   |                     ++++++++++++++

warning: unused import: `crate::b::value`
  --> src/main.rs:14:5

14 | use crate::b::value;

annotations.note_md: line 13: the first import already claimed the name `value` in this scope.
line 14: a second item can't take the same name, or `value()` would be ambiguous.

screens.heading: Rename an import with `as`
screens.text_md:
`as` gives an import a different name in this scope. `FirstPoint` is still the type `first::Point`, under another name: no new type is created, and the original keeps its name in `first`.

The Book renames `std::io::Result` to `IoResult` the same way, so it can sit next to `std::fmt::Result`. Pick a new name that still says where the item comes from.

screens.heading: Combine imports with a nested path
screens.text_md:
When several imports share a prefix, a **nested path** lists the different endings in braces. `use std::cmp::{self, Ordering};` replaces two lines, `use std::cmp;` and `use std::cmp::Ordering;`. `self` inside the braces imports the module the prefix names, so `shapes::area` and `cmp::max` work here.

Braces can appear at any segment: the Book writes `use std::{cmp::Ordering, io};` for two different modules of `std`.

screens.heading: A glob imports every public name
screens.text_md:
The **glob** `*` imports every public item of a module at once. Use it sparingly: a reader can't see where `RED` was defined, and if `colors` later gains an item with the same name as one of yours, the import becomes ambiguous.

Globs are mostly used to bring everything under test into a test module, which Chapter 11 shows. Like any import, a glob can't reach private items.

screens.heading: Re-export a deliberate public API
screens.text_md:
`pub use` imports a name and makes that name public, so other crates can use it at the new path. This is called **re-exporting**. The binary writes `module_lab::Tag` even though `implementation` is private: the library chose to expose `Tag` at its root.

The library can now reorganize its private modules without breaking any caller.

question.general_md: Correct. `Ticket` is another name for `model::Tag`, so `&t` fits `describe`'s parameter. `t.0` is "rust", whose length is 4.

wrong_answers.why_md: `as` doesn't create a new type. `Ticket` and `model::Tag` are the same struct, so `&t` has type `&model::Tag`.
`println!` only borrows `t.0`, and `describe` takes `&t`, so nothing is moved out of `t`.

screens.heading: Imports should show where names come from
screens.text_md:
Good imports keep each name's origin visible. Functions are called through their parent module, `math::square`, so a reader knows to look in `math`. Types are imported by name, `Square`, because type names are rarely ambiguous.

Save `as` for real name collisions, and globs for tests. Neither changes what an item is or who may use it.

lessons.title: Modules in separate files
lessons.objective_md: Move module bodies into matching files while retaining one declaration, exact public paths and separate library/binary roots.

screens.heading: Before: the module body is inline
screens.text_md:
So far every module's body has been written inline, between the braces of its `mod` block. That's fine for small modules, but as a crate grows, one long `src/lib.rs` gets hard to navigate.

Next, this same `garden` module moves into its own file. Watch the path `module_lab::garden::beds`: it won't change.

screens.heading: After: the body moves to src/garden.rs

coming_from.c: `mod garden;` is not `#include`: the file isn't pasted in as text, and there's no header. It's compiled as part of the same crate, and its items keep their module path and privacy.
coming_from.go: Go compiles every `.go` file in a package's directory automatically. Rust compiles only files reached through `mod` declarations from the crate root, so an undeclared file is left out of the build.
coming_from.java: Like Java packages, the file location must match the module's place in the tree. Unlike Java or C#, a file isn't compiled just because it's in the project: its parent's `mod garden;` pulls it in.
coming_from.js: Unlike ES modules, where every file is a module and `import` loads it, a Rust file joins the crate only through a `mod` declaration in its parent. `use` never loads files; it shortens paths.
coming_from.python: In Python, `garden.py` is a module just because it exists. In Rust, `src/garden.rs` is ignored until a parent declares `mod garden;`, and that declaration decides where it sits in the module tree.

steps.caption_md: Ending the declaration with `;` instead of a `{ ... }` block tells the compiler the body is in another file. The declaration stays in `src/lib.rs`, because it's still what puts `garden` into the module tree.
steps.visual_md: Tree: crate (src/lib.rs) → garden, drawn with a dashed body "body in another file".

steps.caption_md: The compiler looks for the body in a file named after the module, next to the file that declared it: `src/garden.rs`. The file holds only what was between the braces; it doesn't repeat `mod garden`.
steps.visual_md: File src/garden.rs attached to node garden; garden → beds.

steps.caption_md: The path is the same as before the move, so callers don't change. Files are only where code is stored; the module tree decides the paths.
steps.visual_md: Path module_lab → garden → beds highlighted; beds() returns 2; stdout: 2.

screens.heading: A child module's file goes in its parent's folder
screens.text_md:
`vegetables` is declared inside `garden`, so its file goes in a folder named after the parent: `src/garden/vegetables.rs`. The folders mirror the module tree, so `crate::garden::vegetables` lives in `src/garden/vegetables.rs`.

`garden` itself still lives in `src/garden.rs`, next to the new `src/garden/` folder.

screens.heading: The file is in the wrong folder
screens.text_md:
The body was saved as `src/vegetables.rs`, but `pub mod vegetables;` is written in `src/garden.rs`, so the compiler looks for `src/garden/vegetables.rs`. A file in the wrong folder isn't found; it's never guessed.

`src/vegetables.rs` would be the right place only for a `mod vegetables;` declared in `src/lib.rs`, at the crate root.

1 | pub mod vegetables;

question.prompt_md: `src/lib.rs` declares `mod garden;` and `src/garden.rs` declares `mod beds;`. Where does the compiler look for the body of `beds` first?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `src/beds.rs` is the place for a `mod beds;` declared at the crate root. This one is declared inside `garden` (E0583 if it's put here).
Correct. A child module's file goes in a folder named after its parent: `crate::garden::beds` lives in `src/garden/beds.rs`.
Not quite. `src/garden.rs` is a file, not a folder. The folder for `garden`'s children is `src/garden/`, next to it.

screens.heading: Declare a module once, then use paths
screens.text_md:
Each module file is declared exactly once, in its parent: `src/lib.rs` declares both `garden` and `tools`. Other modules reach `tools` with a path or a `use`, so `src/garden.rs` writes `use crate::tools;`.

`mod` is not an import. A `mod tools;` inside `src/garden.rs` would declare a new module, `crate::garden::tools`, and look for `src/garden/tools.rs`.

screens.heading: The older mod.rs layout
screens.text_md:
Rust also accepts an older layout: the body of `garden` in `src/garden/mod.rs`. Prefer `src/garden.rs`: with the older style, a large project ends up with many files all named `mod.rs`, which are hard to tell apart in an editor's tabs.

You may mix the two styles in one crate, one module at a time. The next screen shows what happens when one module has both files.

screens.heading: Two files for one module
screens.text_md:
One `mod garden;` declaration can have only one body. With both `src/garden.rs` and `src/garden/mod.rs` present, the compiler can't know which you meant, so it stops with E0761 instead of picking one.

Delete or rename one of the two files. Here, keeping `src/garden.rs` follows the modern style.

error[E0761]: file for module `garden` found at both "src/garden.rs" and "src/garden/mod.rs"
 --> src/lib.rs:1:1
  |
1 | pub mod garden;
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = help: delete or rename one of them to remove the ambiguity

annotations.note_md: `src/lib.rs` line 1: one declaration, two possible bodies.

annotations.mark: delete or rename one of them
annotations.note_md: keep one file; the compiler won't pick one for you.

question.general_md: Correct. `vegetables.rs` is in `src/garden/`, matching its declaration inside `garden`. The re-export makes `count` reachable as `module_lab::plants`, which returns 3, plus 1.

wrong_answers.why_md: `garden` is private, but the binary never names it. `pub use` publishes `count` at the library's root as `plants`.
`vegetables` is declared in `src/garden.rs`, so `src/garden/vegetables.rs` is exactly where its body belongs.

screens.heading: A public API that survives a file move
screens.text_md:
The code lives in a private module file, `src/implementation.rs`, and `pub use` publishes `answer` at the library's root. Callers write `module_lab::answer()` and never see the file layout.

The chapter project and the library-manager milestone use this structure: files reflect responsibilities, and public paths describe the supported API.

question.prompt_md: The library declares `mod book;` in `src/lib.rs`. Then `src/main.rs` also writes `mod book;`. What happens?

options.text_md: The binary crate compiles `src/book.rs` again as its own, separate `book` module.
The binary gets a shortcut to the library's `book` module.
The two crates merge into one, sharing a single `book` module.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Each crate builds its own module tree from its own root. The binary's `crate::book` is a second copy, and its types are different types from the library's.
Not quite. `mod` declares a module; it never imports one. The binary reaches the library's items through the crate name, `module_lab::...`, if they're public.
Not quite. The library and the binary stay separate crates with separate roots, even inside one package.

summary: `mod garden;` with a semicolon declares the module and loads its body from `src/garden.rs`; moving a body into a file doesn't change any paths.
A child module's file goes in a folder named after its parent: `crate::garden::vegetables` lives in `src/garden/vegetables.rs` (E0583 if it's elsewhere).
Declare each module once, in its parent; other code reaches it with paths or `use`, never a second `mod`.
`src/garden/mod.rs` is the older layout; prefer `src/garden.rs`, and never keep both (E0761).

questions.prompt_md: What describes a Cargo package?

options.text_md: One mandatory Rust file with no manifest.
A `Cargo.toml` manifest and one or more crate targets.
A runtime object that owns heap data.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `rustc` can compile a single file, but Cargo only knows a package through its `Cargo.toml` manifest.
Correct. The manifest describes the package, and Cargo builds each crate root it finds (`src/main.rs`, `src/lib.rs`, ...) as a separate crate.
Not quite. This mixes up build organisation with ownership. A package exists only at build time; it is never a value in the running program.

questions.prompt_md: Which file is the root of a package's library crate by convention?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `Cargo.lock` records the exact dependency versions Cargo resolved. It is not Rust source.
Not quite. Extra binaries live in the `src/bin/` directory. A file named `src/bin.rs` has no special meaning to Cargo.
Correct. When `src/lib.rs` exists, Cargo builds a library crate from it, named after the package.

questions.prompt_md: Match each conventional package file to its role.

explanations.text_md: `Cargo.toml` names the package and its dependencies.
`src/lib.rs` starts the library crate whose public items other crates can call.
`src/main.rs` starts the binary crate named after the package.
each file in `src/bin/` starts its own executable, here one called `admin`. It is not a module of `main.rs`.

questions.prompt_md: One package can contain both `src/main.rs` and `src/lib.rs`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Cargo builds `src/lib.rs` as the library crate and `src/main.rs` as a binary crate of the same package, and the binary can call the library by the package's name.
Not quite. This treats a package as if it were a single crate. A package may hold at most one library but any number of binaries, so the two roots sit side by side.

questions.prompt_md: Every `.rs` file inside `src/` is automatically compiled as its own crate.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. This confuses files with crates. Only crate roots (`src/main.rs`, `src/lib.rs`, files in `src/bin/`) start crates; a file such as `src/garden.rs` is compiled only when a `mod garden;` declaration pulls it into a crate as a module.
Correct. Crate roots start crates. Every other source file is a module that some crate has to declare.

questions.prompt_md: A library crate must define a `main` function.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `main` is the entry point of an executable. A library is never run on its own; other crates call its public functions, so `src/lib.rs` usually has no `main`.
Correct. Only binary crates need `main`. A library only provides items for other crates to use.

questions.prompt_md: Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text_md: A package can include library and binary targets.
A binary's entry point is its `main` function.
A package has at most one library target.
Every module file is a separate crate.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `src/lib.rs` and `src/main.rs` (plus any files in `src/bin/`) can share one package.
Correct. Running an executable starts at its `main`.
Correct. Cargo allows one library per package, but any number of binaries.
Not quite. A module file belongs to the crate whose `mod` declaration includes it. It never becomes an independent crate.

questions.prompt_md: A package has `src/lib.rs`, `src/main.rs` and `src/bin/admin.rs`. Which crates does Cargo build?

options.text_md: One binary containing all three files.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Only `src/lib.rs` is a library root; `src/main.rs` and `src/bin/admin.rs` are executables.
Not quite. Each root starts a separate crate. Cargo never merges roots into one crate; the binaries reach the library by its crate name.
Correct. `lib.rs` is the library, `main.rs` is the default binary and `bin/admin.rs` is a second binary named `admin`.

questions.prompt_md: What does `mod tools { ... }` create?

options.text_md: A child module in the current crate's module tree.
A runtime value that must be cloned to share.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Packages come from `Cargo.toml`. `mod` only adds a named section inside the crate being compiled.
Correct. `tools` becomes a child of the module where it is written, and its items are reached as `tools::name`.
Not quite. A module groups names at compile time. Nothing about it exists as a value at run time, so ownership rules don't apply to it.

questions.prompt_md: A function inside a module is written without `pub`. Where can it be called?

options.text_md: Only inside its own function body.
From any crate that depends on this one.
Inside the module that contains it and that module's descendants.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Privacy is about modules, not function bodies. Every other function in the same module can call it.
Not quite. That describes a `pub` item on a public path. Without `pub`, the item stays hidden even from the parent module.
Correct. Items are private to their parent module, and child modules can see their ancestors' private items.

questions.prompt_md: A library has `mod hidden { pub fn run() {} }` (no `pub` on the module). Can another crate call `hidden::run()`?

options.text_md: No. The private module `hidden` blocks the path.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Return types affect how values move, not whether a path is visible.
Not quite. `pub` on an item does not make its ancestors public. Every module along the path must also be reachable.
Correct. Outside the library's root module, `hidden` is private, so its public contents can't be reached through it (E0603).

questions.prompt_md: A `pub fn` can call a private function defined in the same module.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Privacy limits who outside the module can name the helper. Code inside the module, including its public functions, uses it freely.
Not quite. This would make private helpers useless. Hiding a helper is about callers outside the module, not about its neighbours.

questions.prompt_md: A child module may use a private item defined in its parent module.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Privacy hides an item from code outside its module, and a child module is inside its parent. `super::helper()` works even when `helper` has no `pub`.
Not quite. This reverses the rule. A parent can't see its child's private items, but a child can see its ancestors' private items.

Not quite. Paths follow the module tree that `mod` declarations build, not folders on disk at run time.
Not quite. Each crate has its own root. In `src/main.rs`, `crate` is the binary's root, not the library's.

problems.title: One package, two crates
problems.description_md:
The starter package has only a binary crate: `src/main.rs` defines `greeting` and prints its result. Give the package a second crate. Create the library crate root `src/lib.rs` and move `greeting` into it as `pub fn greeting(name: &str) -> String`, which returns exactly `Ready, {name}!` with no newline and `name` unchanged. Then change `src/main.rs` so it defines only `main`, which calls the library as `module_lab::greeting("reader")` and prints the result followed by one newline.

Keep the supplied `Cargo.toml` (package `module-lab`), so the library crate's name is `module_lab`. Tests call `crate::greeting` inside the library crate and also run the binary.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::greeting("Ada")
Expected:   "Ready, Ada!".to_string()
The library crate formats a present name.

Expression: crate::greeting("Bo")
Expected:   "Ready, Bo!".to_string()
Another name is copied unchanged into the owned result.

Expression: crate::greeting("")
Expected:   "Ready, !".to_string()
Only the fixed text remains for an empty name.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `name` is at most 100,000 UTF-8 bytes; return it unchanged, including whitespace.
- The package has exactly one library target (`src/lib.rs`) and one binary target (`src/main.rs`); no `[lib]` or `[[bin]]` sections are added.

`render` skips `None` entries and labels that normalize to empty text, numbers the remaining labels from 1 in input order, and emits exactly `"{number}. {normalized}\n"` for each. problems.title: Split the vending machine into modules
problems.description_md:
**Part 1**

The starter is the Accepted Chapter 6 vending reference in one file, `src/lib.rs`. Create `src/item.rs`, `src/coin.rs` and `src/machine.rs`, and move (do not copy) `Item` with its `impl` into `item.rs`, `Coin` with its `impl` into `coin.rs`, and `Machine` with its `impl` into `machine.rs`. Keep every variant, public field, derive, receiver, signature, price and transaction rule unchanged.

**Part 2**

`src/lib.rs` becomes a crate root that only declares the three public modules (`pub mod item;`, `pub mod coin;`, `pub mod machine;`) and re-exports `Item`, `Coin` and `Machine` with `pub use`. An external crate can then write `vending::Machine` or `vending::machine::Machine`, and both paths name the same type.

**Part 3**

In `machine.rs`, bring `Item` and `Coin` into scope with a `use crate::…` declaration. Move the change calculation of `buy` into a private module-level function `fn change_for(credit: u32, item: Item) -> Option<u32>` that returns `Some(credit - price)`, or `None` when the credit is short. It is not marked `pub`, so code outside `machine` (including an external crate) cannot call it.

**Part 4**

The Chapter 6 transaction fixtures and the deterministic operation suite run against the refactored crate through the crate-root re-exports. No binary, UI, file persistence or new products are added.

problems.random_md:
Reset the 32-bit LCG to seed `0x06010000` once. next() updates state = (1664525 × state + 1013904223) mod 2^32; pick(k) = (next() >> 16) % k. Generate 300 cases. Per case, draw stocks[0], stocks[1], stocks[2] with pick(6), then credit=next(). Perform 20 operations; each draws op=pick(3), then arg=pick(4), even for refund. op 0 inserts [Nickel,Dime,Quarter,Dollar][arg]; op 1 buys [Tea,Coffee,Water][arg%3]; op 2 refunds. Compute the model using unbounded integers: insertion succeeds only if credit+coin <= 4294967295; purchase succeeds only if selected stock > 0 and credit >= price; successful purchase returns all change and clears credit; rejection preserves the entire state. Refund clears credit. Compare return values, credit and all three stock slots after every operation.

This is the Chapter 6 regression suite, unchanged and carried forward through the crate-root re-exports (`vending::Machine`, `vending::Item`, `vending::Coin`). It is regression coverage, not a new Chapter 7 feature.

problems.description_md:
**Part 1**

The starter is the Accepted LM6 program in one file, `src/main.rs`: the fee constants and helpers, the title helpers, `Book`, `Status`, `Member` and the banner/menu `main`. Create `src/lib.rs` and move (do not copy) the constants, `due_day`, `days_late`, `late_fee_cents` and `format_cents` into `src/fees.rs`; `normalize_title`, `sort_key` and `title_matches` into `src/text.rs`; `Book`, `Status` and both `impl Book` blocks into `src/book.rs`; and `Member` with its `impl` into `src/member.rs`. Preserve every public field, derive, method, signature and behavior.

**Part 2**

`src/lib.rs` declares `pub mod fees;`, `pub mod text;`, `pub mod book;` and `pub mod member;`, and re-exports `book::{Book, Status}` and `member::Member` at the root. External callers can use `library::Book` and `library::book::Book` interchangeably.

**Part 3**

`book.rs` imports what it needs (`due_day`, `days_late`, `late_fee_cents`, `normalize_title` and `Member`) with one nested `use crate::{…};` declaration. Those imports are private to `book`, so `library::book::due_day` is not a public path; the public path is `library::fees::due_day`. `src/main.rs` keeps only `use std::io;` and the unchanged banner/menu `fn main`: it declares no modules and defines no library items, so the binary crate and the library crate stay separate. No catalogue commands are connected to the menu yet.

**Part 4**

All LM6 transaction fixtures, earlier numeric/title regressions and the exact menu transcripts run against the package. No catalogue, new commands, changed checkout rules or new error types are added.

Reset the 32-bit LCG to seed `0x06020000` once; next() uses the recurrence above. Generate cases i=0..299. Each case consumes exactly three draws: member_id=next(), due=next(), raw_day=next(). Let mode=i%10 and premium=(i//10)%2==1. Let limit be 6 for premium, otherwise 3. Book metadata is (id=1,title="x",author="y",year=1); member name is "A". Modes 0–3 start Available and call checkout at today=raw_day%4294967268; initial borrowed is respectively 0, limit, 255, limit-1. For return modes override due_day to 100 (the draw is still consumed); choose today from [99,100,101,107,108,143,144,4294967295][(i//10)%8]. The independent oracle uses state and limit comparisons; successful checkout increments once and sets due today+14/28. Rejected operations preserve both complete records. Matching returns produce Some(min(2000,25*min(late,7)+50*max(late-7,0))) with late=max(today-100,0), set Available, and floor the decremented count at zero. Compare the result and complete Book and Member records after every call.
